title: Molecular-Orbital Theory Does not Predict a Stable Diatomic Helium Molecule
lead: Bond order counts the net bonding electrons in a molecular orbital diagram and predicts which species hold together. The section applies it to the molecules and ions built from 1s orbitals, ending with the helium dimer.
objectives: Using bond order as a metric for the existance of molecules
notes: The book names no author for this page, which is shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Figure 9.8.1 is printed as CC BY-SA-NC with no author, and Example 9.8.1's two diagrams, which the book gives no credit for, are folded into it.

exercises.prompt:
The $\mathrm{H_2^{2−}}$ Ion

Use a molecular orbital energy-level diagram to predict the valence-electron configuration and bond order of the $\mathrm{H_2^{2−}}$ ion. Is this a stable species?

answer.solution: $\mathrm{H_2^{2−}}$ has a valence electron configuration of $\left (\sigma _{1s} \right )^{2}\left (\sigma _{1s}^{\star } \right )^{2}$ with a bond order of 0. It is therefore predicted to be unstable.

footnotes.html: Figure 9.8.1b and the paragraph are about He<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, the ion with three valence electrons; He<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup> has two and is the subject of Example 9.8.1.
With two electrons in each orbital the configuration is $\left(\sigma_{1s}\right)^{2}\left(\sigma^{*}_{1s}\right)^{2}$, as Table 9.8.1 gives it.

The measured binding energy of He<sub>2</sub> is about 1.1 mK, or $9 \times 10^{-6}$ kJ/mol (Grisenti and coworkers, 2000), and the LM2M2 potential of Figure 9.8.2 gives 1.3 mK; the $4.6 \times 10^{-5}$ kJ/mol printed here and in Table 9.8.1 is about five times too large. Either way the bond is some forty million times weaker than H<sub>2</sub>'s 436 kJ/mol, not 5,000 times.
